details:
ORBITAL

Developed by Team SKYX

Project Summary

ORBITAL is an interactive web platform that transforms NASA SPHEREx infrared sky observations into an accessible, verifiable exploration experience for both the public and researchers.

By automating the retrieval, quality inspection, and multi-epoch comparison of real FITS astronomical data, ORBITAL helps users distinguish genuine celestial motion and variability from imaging artifacts, transforming raw space data into transparent, documented scientific evidence.

Project Details

1. The Challenge

NASA's SPHEREx mission maps the entire sky every six months across 102 infrared spectral bands, generating an extraordinary volume of astronomical observations.

However, the challenge of astronomical discovery extends beyond collecting data. Reliable interpretation is essential.

Not every visual change between two observations represents a moving or variable celestial object. Saturated stars, damaged pixels, source confusion, and instrumental artifacts can produce misleading signals and false detections.

Furthermore, raw astronomical FITS files require specialized software and scientific expertise, creating barriers for students, educators, citizen scientists, and the general public.

ORBITAL addresses these challenges by making authentic astronomical data accessible, scientifically interpretable, and independently verifiable.

2. Our Solution: What ORBITAL Does and How It Works

ORBITAL implements a structured five-stage scientific pipeline that connects raw NASA observations with interactive exploration and evidence-based analysis.

Stage 1: Search and Data Retrieval

Users can enter celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) or explore the sky above their geographic location.

ORBITAL queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) to retrieve authentic SPHEREx FITS observations.

Stage 2: Automated Data Inspection

The Python backend automatically examines:

  • FITS headers and observation metadata.
  • World Coordinate System (WCS) information.
  • Observation timestamps.
  • Detector and wavelength information.
  • IMAGE, VARIANCE, and FLAGS data layers.

This process helps identify compromised observations before scientific measurements are performed.

Stage 3: Visual and Comparison Laboratory

Users can compare astronomical observations from different epochs through three interactive visualization methods:

  • Blink Mode: Alternates between observations to reveal positional or brightness changes.
  • Overlay Mode: Combines observations to highlight differences.
  • Sequence Mode: Displays observations chronologically to examine changes over time.

These tools help users investigate possible celestial motion and variability.

Stage 4: Dual-Mode Exploration

ORBITAL provides two complementary experiences.

Explorer Mode — For Everyone

Simplifies complex infrared imagery into an intuitive, interactive experience supported by AI-assisted explanations in accessible language.

It enables students, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts to explore real astronomical observations without requiring advanced scientific knowledge.

Scientific Mode — For Researchers

Provides access to advanced scientific information, including:

  • Original FITS metadata.
  • Pixel-quality masks.
  • WCS information.
  • Multi-band spectral samples.
  • Astrometric motion tracks.
  • Observation quality indicators.

This mode supports deeper scientific inspection and transparent interpretation.

Stage 5: Verification and Evidence Reporting

Potential detections are compared against independent astronomical catalogs, including ESA Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD.

ORBITAL generates structured Evidence Reports documenting measurement uncertainty, verification results, and known limitations.

Unvalidated results are explicitly labelled INCONCLUSIVE, and no unverified candidate is presented as a confirmed discovery.

3. Scientific Discovery Workbench

Beyond astronomical visualization, ORBITAL includes a dedicated Scientific Discovery Workbench designed for researchers who want to develop, execute, and compare their own analysis methods using authentic observations.

Research Environment

The Workbench includes:

  • An integrated Python code editor.
  • A terminal for scientific workflows.
  • An interactive FITS image viewer.
  • Ready-made experimental templates.

Supported research areas include source detection, astrometry, photometry, image registration, saturation analysis, and motion fitting.

Quality-Gate Experimentation

Researchers can investigate how different pixel-acceptance policies affect astronomical measurements.

The system preserves the original official data-quality flags while allowing controlled experimental comparisons.

Algorithm Comparison and Reproducibility

Multiple scientific algorithms can be tested side by side using the same observational data.

Each experiment records its source code, parameters, and original-file SHA-256 hashes to support reproducibility and scientific auditing.

Secure Execution

Researcher code executes inside an isolated container environment with:

  • Read-only access to original data.
  • CPU, memory, disk, and execution-time limits.
  • Network restrictions.
  • Protection against access to server secrets.

Scientific Review

Experimental outputs are separated from official scientific evidence.

Results can enter official Evidence Reports only after explicit review by an identified reviewer.

This design encourages experimentation without compromising the integrity of validated results.

4. Proof of Concept and Scientific Validation

ORBITAL has been tested using authentic NASA SPHEREx FITS observations rather than synthetic demonstration data.

Primary Validation: Van Maanen's Star

The system processed 23 real SPHEREx observations of Van Maanen's Star.

After applying quality checks:

  • 23 observations were processed.
  • Compromised frames were rejected using quality flags.
  • 20 exposures were accepted for astrometric measurement.
  • The recovered proper motion was consistent with independent Gaia DR3 reference data, subject to documented validation limitations.

This case demonstrates ORBITAL's ability to support scientifically grounded analysis of real astronomical observations.

Additional Scientific Cases

Barnard's Star — INCONCLUSIVE

Strong stellar brightness produces saturated source cores, limiting reliable positional measurements.

Rather than generating unsupported conclusions, ORBITAL identifies the affected data and documents the limitations.

LAWD 37 — INCONCLUSIVE

The target fails the nearby-source identity verification check, preventing a sufficiently reliable identification for the intended measurement.

These cases demonstrate an important scientific principle underlying ORBITAL:

Identifying why a measurement cannot be trusted is itself a valuable scientific result.

5. Benefits and Intended Impact

Educational and Public Impact

ORBITAL makes real NASA astronomical observations accessible to people without specialized astronomy training.

Its bilingual English-Arabic interface supports inclusive learning and encourages students to engage directly with scientific data.

Scientific and Research Impact

Researchers gain access to a transparent and reproducible environment for investigating apparent astronomical changes, evaluating data quality, and testing alternative analysis methods before making scientific claims.

Local Impact: Sultanate of Oman

ORBITAL aims to expand access to space science and practical astronomical data analysis among students, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts in Oman.

Its architecture is also designed to support potential future integration with local satellite datasets.

Global Impact

ORBITAL encourages international citizen-science participation by enabling users to share celestial coordinates, collaboratively investigate anomalies, and explore authentic astronomical observations.

The long-term vision is to help bridge the gap between professional astronomy and public scientific participation.

6. Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware, and Software

Backend Development

  • Python 3.12: Backend development and scientific processing.
  • FastAPI: Backend API framework.
  • Astropy: FITS processing and WCS transformations.
  • Photutils: Astronomical source detection and photometric analysis.
  • SciPy and NumPy: Numerical and scientific computation.
  • Matplotlib: Scientific visualization.
  • pandas: Data processing and analysis.

Frontend Development

  • React: Interactive web interface.
  • TypeScript: Application development.
  • Vite: Frontend development and build tooling.
  • Aladin Lite: Interactive astronomical sky visualization.
  • CodeMirror: Integrated scientific code editor.

Infrastructure and Security

  • Docker Compose for container orchestration.
  • nginx for web serving and reverse proxy functionality.
  • Isolated laboratory containers for researcher code execution.
  • Allow-listing egress proxy for controlled network access.

Testing and Validation

  • Python unittest suites, including 38 existing tests and 21 Workbench acceptance tests.
  • Playwright for browser-based testing.

Hardware

Development was performed using ordinary personal computers.

No specialized astronomical hardware is required to access the platform, which operates through a standard web browser.

7. Creativity and Innovation

ORBITAL combines historical astronomical discovery techniques with modern infrared observations, interactive web technology, and reproducible scientific computing.

Reimagining the Blink Comparator

The project draws inspiration from Clyde Tombaugh's 1930 discovery of Pluto, which relied on comparing astronomical photographic plates.

ORBITAL adapts this principle to modern multi-epoch infrared observations from SPHEREx.

False-Positive-Aware Discovery

Unlike visualization tools focused primarily on displaying astronomical objects, ORBITAL emphasizes evaluating whether apparent changes are scientifically trustworthy.

It exposes saturation, damaged pixels, source confusion, and quality-flag limitations rather than hiding them.

One Platform, Multiple Audiences

ORBITAL combines an accessible Explorer Mode with advanced Scientific Mode and a dedicated research Workbench.

This allows beginners and researchers to engage with the same underlying astronomical observations at different levels of complexity.

Traceable Scientific Evidence

Scientific measurements are linked to their source observations and processing steps.

Data and results are explicitly categorized as real, experimental, simulated, or test, helping prevent confusion between verified evidence and demonstrations.

8. Factors Our Team Considered

Scientific Accuracy and Honesty

Our team prioritized reliable interpretation over unsupported discovery claims.

Catalog matches do not automatically establish source identity, and agreement between algorithms does not necessarily prove accuracy.

Uncertainty and limitations are explicitly documented.

Data Integrity

Original FITS observations remain unchanged.

Cryptographic hashes support file verification, and official quality flags are preserved throughout experimental analysis.

Research Security

The Workbench is designed to isolate user-executed code through containerization, restricted resources, controlled networking, and protection of server credentials.

Accessibility and Inclusion

The platform is designed for users with different levels of scientific experience.

A bilingual interface and browser-based architecture help reduce technical and educational barriers.

Instrumental and Observational Limitations

The team explicitly considered:

  • Stellar saturation.
  • Missing or corrupted pixels.
  • Limited image cutout sizes.
  • Source confusion.
  • Astrometric uncertainty.
  • Observation quality differences.
  • False-positive detections.

Rather than concealing these challenges, ORBITAL incorporates them into its scientific verification workflow.

NASA Data and Scientific References

9. NASA and Space-Agency Datasets

NASA SPHEREx Mission Data

Authentic multi-epoch infrared FITS observations obtained through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), including IMAGE, VARIANCE, FLAGS, and WCS metadata.

ESA Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3)

Independent astrometric reference data used to evaluate source positions and validate proper-motion measurements.

SIMBAD Astronomical Database (CDS)

Used for celestial-object cross-identification and background-source verification.

10. Technical Standards and Scientific References

FITS and WCS Standards

Astronomical data standards used for image parsing, metadata interpretation, and celestial coordinate transformations through the Astropy ecosystem.

SPHEREx Mission Specifications and Explanatory Supplement

NASA, Caltech, and JPL mission documentation covering:

  • Six detector arrays.
  • Approximately 25.2 million detector pixels.
  • 102 spectral channels.
  • Wavelength coverage of 0.75–5.0 μm.
  • Instrumental data-quality flag definitions.

Historical Scientific Inspiration

Clyde Tombaugh's discovery of Pluto in 1930 at Lowell Observatory using blink-comparator photographic plate analysis.

Conclusion

ORBITAL is more than an astronomical image viewer. It is an accessible, reproducible, and scientifically responsible platform that connects authentic NASA space observations with public exploration and research.

By combining interactive visualization, automated quality inspection, independent catalog verification, and a secure scientific experimentation environment, ORBITAL helps users understand not only what changes in the sky, but also whether those changes can be trusted.

Developed by Team SKYX, ORBITAL aims to make astronomical exploration more accessible, transparent, and scientifically meaningful for communities in Oman and around the world.
